Asaiah
a-sā´yah
n. (a servant of king Josiah sent to Huldah; also Levites and a Simeonite of the same name; Hebrew Asayah)
Hebrew Asayah, ‘the LORD hath made’ or ‘wrought’ — from asah, to do or make, with the divine name.

Biblical Definition

Asaiah is named among the five men king Josiah sent when the book of the law was found in the house of the LORD. The king had rent his clothes at the reading, and he commanded Hilkiah, Ahikam, Abdon, Shaphan the scribe, and “Asaiah a servant of the king's” (2Ch 34:20) to enquire of the LORD concerning the words of the book. The delegation went to Huldah the prophetess, and brought back the word that the LORD would indeed bring evil upon the place, but not in Josiah's days, because his heart was tender and he had humbled himself. Asaiah is styled simply the king's servant — the layman in a company of priests and scribes — and he is trusted with the errand on which the reformation turned. The name belongs to others: a Levite of the sons of Merari (1Ch 6:30), the firstborn of the Shilonites who dwelt at Jerusalem after the captivity (1Ch 9:5), and a prince of Simeon among those who drove out the Hamites from their pasture (1Ch 4:36).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) does not enter Asaiah; the name is fixed by the Hebrew text as, the LORD hath made.

expand to see more

The proper name is not entered in Webster's 1828 dictionary.

ASAIAH. A servant of Josiah, sent with Hilkiah and Shaphan to enquire of the LORD.

The name signifies, Jehovah hath made, or wrought.

The parallel passage in 2 Kings 22:12 spells the name Asahiah.

The name is borne also by a Levite of Merari and by a prince of the tribe of Simeon.

Key Scripture

2Ch 34:20 — "And the king commanded Hilkiah, and Ahikam the son of Shaphan, and Abdon the son of Micah, and Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah a servant of the king's, saying,"

1Ch 6:30 — "Shimea his son, Haggiah his son, Asaiah his son."

1Ch 9:5 — "And of the Shilonites; Asaiah the firstborn, and his sons."

1Ch 4:36 — "And Elioenai, and Jaakobah, and Jeshohaiah, and Asaiah, and Adiel, and Jesimiel, and Benaiah,"

Modern Corruption

Josiah's response to the recovered book is admired as sincerity of feeling, when the text presents it as submission to a word that condemned him.

expand to see more

The scene Asaiah was sent into is often reduced to an emotional one: a young king moved by an old book. What actually happens is harder and better. The law is read, and it pronounces against Judah; Josiah does not soften it, does not enquire whether it applies to his times, and does not look for a second opinion. He sends to a prophetess to learn how bad it truly is. The errand assumes the book has authority over the throne that received it. That is the reformation in miniature, and it is why the LORD's answer singles out the king's tender heart — not his feelings, but his yielding.

The principle to recover is the standing of an ordinary servant in such a moment. Asaiah is the one man in the five with no office named — not priest, not scribe, not son of a notable — and he goes with the rest to hear a word that will govern the kingdom. Reformation has never been carried by clergy alone. It moves through households and servants and men whose only description in the record is that they belonged to somebody and were sent. The name says the LORD hath made; the errand shows what He makes such men for.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Asayah (H6222), the LORD hath made; from asah (H6213), to do, make, work, and Yah, the divine name.

expand to see more

Hebrew Asayah (H6222) — Asaiah; 2 Chronicles 34:20, 1 Chronicles 6:30, 1 Chronicles 9:5.

Hebrew asah (H6213) — to do, make, fashion, accomplish.

Hebrew ebed (H5650) — a servant; the description given him by the Chronicler.

Hebrew sepher ha-torah — the book of the law found in the house of the LORD; 2 Chronicles 34:15.

2 Kings 22:12 gives the same man's name as Asahiah.

Usage

"“Asaiah a servant of the king's” — the layman on the reformation errand."

"“Asaiah the firstborn” — of the Shilonites who dwelt at Jerusalem."

"“Enquire of the LORD” — the book is treated as having authority over the throne."
